asm:segment:households_without_adequate_.what: share of local cold burden in households_without_adequate_heat
asm:segment:households_without_adequate_.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file

asm:segment:low_income:cold.what: share of local cold burden in low_income
asm:segment:low_income:cold.basis: Base as above. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 - energy prices raise winter mortality; UK Winter Fuel Payment reduced cold mortality (direction cited); 1.5 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:low_income:heat.what: share of local heat burden in low_income
asm:segment:low_income:heat.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 B17001 share below poverty. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 - income support (minimum wage, cash transfers) reduces heat mortality, i.e. low income raises vulnerability (direction cited); 1.5 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:mental_illness_or_substance_.what: share of local heat burden in mental_illness_or_substance_use
asm:segment:mental_illness_or_substance_.basis: Coded part: ~25% of CA death certificates listing heat-related illness (2018-2022) also list drug overdose (CDC data reported by KFF Health News / California Healthline, 2023). Uncoded part: population share 0.05 ASSUMPTION x 2.0 ASSUMPTION

asm:segment:older_adults:cold.what: share of local cold burden in older_adults
asm:segment:older_adults:cold.basis: Base as above. Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 sec.3 - relative cold risk rises with age (direction cited); 1.1 is ASSUMPTION; capped so share <= 1 | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:older_adults:heat.what: share of local heat burden in older_adults
asm:segment:older_adults:heat.basis: Base: CDPH final death profiles, residence, all causes, 2018/2019/2023/2024 (65+ = share of deaths). Multiplier: Burke, Wilson et al. 2026 sec.3 - relative heat risk falls with age but higher baseline mortality offsets it (direction cited); 0.8 is ASSUMPTION | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:outage_exposed:heat.what: share of local heat burden in outage_exposed
asm:segment:outage_exposed:heat.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file; Burke et al.: outages raise hot-day mortality impact 61%/hour above 80F

asm:segment:outdoor_workers:heat.what: share of local heat burden in outdoor_workers
asm:segment:outdoor_workers:heat.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 C24010 natural resources/construction/maintenance share of employed x employment-to-population 0.47 (ASSUMPTION). Multiplier 1.0 ASSUMPTION (high exposure offset by low working-age baseline mortality)

asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.what: share of local cold burden in people_experiencing_homelessness
asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.basis: PIT 2024 population share x all-cause mortality ratio 3.0 ASSUMPTION (hypothermia deaths rising among older unhoused people: KFF Health News 2024) | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.what: share of local heat burden in people_experiencing_homelessness
asm:segment:people_experiencing_homeless.basis: Coded part: ~13% of CA hospitalizations with primary heat-related-illness diagnosis 2017-2021 were homeless (state data reported by KFF Health News / California Healthline, 2023). Uncoded part: PIT 2024 (HUD, CA CoCs) population share x all-cause mortality ratio 3.0 ASSUMPTION. Coded fraction of attributable heat deaths = trigger_fallbacks f_coded | base: state value used as proxy (ASSUMPTION)

asm:segment:recreational_outdoor_users:h.what: share of local heat burden in recreational_outdoor_users
asm:segment:recreational_outdoor_users:h.basis: ASSUMPTION carried from the Phoenix file

asm:segment:renters_or_housing_insecure:.what: share of local heat burden in renters_or_housing_insecure
asm:segment:renters_or_housing_insecure:.basis: Base: ACS 2019-23 B25003 renter-occupied share of households. Multiplier 0.6 ASSUMPTION: cooling standards reach only renters with inadequate cooling

asm:segment:severe_acute_heat_illness_ca.what: share of local heat burden in severe_acute_heat_illness_cases
asm:segment:severe_acute_heat_illness_ca.basis: f_coded x 0.3 (ASSUMPTION: share of coded-type cases reaching EMS alive; Phoenix file used the same 0.3)

calc:agnostic:floor.label: deaths averted per year by the inherited (county and state) plans' firm measures, as written
calc:agnostic:floor.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_inherited measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active))

calc:agnostic:plan.label: deaths averted per year by the plan's firm measures
calc:agnostic:plan.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active))

calc:agnostic:plan_all.label: deaths averted per year by all the plan's firm measures, standing commitments included
calc:agnostic:plan_all.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active)), every firm measure

calc:agnostic:portfolio.label: deaths averted per year by the mix shown (recomputed by the app for the strategies, thresholds and coverage you set)
calc:agnostic:portfolio.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_options (1 − min(1, segment_share × coverage × m) × effect × active)); cost = tier cost × m; at most one threshold per strategy; best mix = multi-start greedy + Pareto filter (pipeline/portfolio.py)

calc:agnostic:residents_best.label: best mix of the stack's measures and the shared menu at the stack's own total cost
calc:agnostic:residents_best.formula: max over a multi-start greedy frontier (stack measures at any timing + shared menu) with cost ≤ stack cost

calc:agnostic:residents_plan.label: deaths averted per year by every plan in the stack (inherited + own), as written
calc:agnostic:residents_plan.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_stack measures (1 − r × active))

calc:agnostic:vintage_2023.label: deaths averted per year by the jurisdiction's own plans in force in 2023, as written, on today's floor, harm and evidence
calc:agnostic:vintage_2023.formula: Σ_days residual_deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − r × active)), measures from the documents in force that year

calc:agnostic:vintage_2026.label: deaths averted per year by the jurisdiction's own plans in force in 2026, as written, on today's floor, harm and evidence
calc:agnostic:vintage_2026.formula: Σ_days residual_deaths_day × (1 − Π_measures (1 − r × active)), measures from the documents in force that year

calc:evidence:floor.label: deaths averted per year by the inherited (county and state) plans' firm measures, as written
calc:evidence:floor.formula: Σ_days deaths_day × (1 − Π_inherited measures (1 − segment_share × coverage × effect × active))

ev:EV01.finding: Three US studies find limited or uncertain mortality effects of heat alerts. Korea: all-cause mortality rose on alert days (decreases for some groups). Japan: ambulance transports rose. Shenzhen: ~10% less heat illness. Germany: no mortality effect. Spain: ~7% fewer hot-day workplace injuries after lowering alert thresholds. Paper concludes alerts alone are insufficient.
ev:EV01.notes: Harmful estimate exists (Korea); keep negative lower bound.
ev:EV01.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV02.finding: No causal health evaluation of cold alerts alone identified (winter forecast lead time reduced car crashes, coded under forecasts).
ev:EV02.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV04.finding: Pakistan RCT: no mortality effect but 38% fewer unscheduled hospital visits. India program: ~41% fewer heat-stroke deaths. China: ~20% less heat illness (not significant). Australia RCT: more protective behavior, less self-reported heat stress. Outdoor worker RCT: non-significant.
ev:EV04.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV05.finding: Paper flags targeted cold information as a critical research priority; no causal studies.
ev:EV05.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV09.finding: California standard: 87% reduction in hot-day injury effect and 33% fewer outdoor-worker heat deaths (neither significant). Dallas rest-break ordinance: no significant effect. El Salvador water/rest: better kidney function (imprecise).
ev:EV09.notes: Applies to worker population only, not whole-population burden.
ev:EV09.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV10.finding: No randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of cooling centers on health identified.
ev:EV10.notes: Very common in plans; key 'popular but unproven' case.
ev:EV10.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV11.finding: US multifamily and Tennessee weatherization: better comfort/self-reported health, imprecise. New Zealand insulation: 11% fewer all-cause, 15% fewer respiratory admissions; related RCT 47% fewer respiratory admissions (not significant). Wales: no clear benefit. East Germany retrofits: 2.9% fewer circulatory hospitalizations 65+, concentrated on coldest days.
ev:EV11.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV13.finding: US: doubling home-heating prices raised winter all-cause mortality ~2%. Japan: higher residential energy prices raised mortality on days below 0C. New Zealand: higher electricity prices raised asthma admissions. China subsidized heating: ~50% lower cold-related mortality. UK Winter Fuel Payment RD: no individual health effect (DiD result coded under income).
ev:EV13.notes: Paper: reducing heating cost reduces cold harm; LIHEAP evaluation is an open research need.
ev:EV13.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV14.finding: Paper notes no evidence on heat for affordability programs.
ev:EV14.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV15.finding: US: each additional outage hour on a day above 80F raised that day's mortality impact by 61%. Australia: outages nearly doubled the effect of extreme heat on ambulance attendances.
ev:EV15.notes: Evidence is on harm of outages, not on a specific reliability program; effect band is a team assumption about avoidable outage-attributable share.
ev:EV15.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV16.finding: Same two studies: no clear effect of outages on cold-related outcomes.
ev:EV16.notes: Uri-type compound events may differ; note but do not override paper.
ev:EV16.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV17.finding: Japan post-Fukushima conservation push raised temperature mortality on hot and cold days; average savings target roughly doubled the mortality impact of a 30C day and raised a 0C day's impact ~10%.
ev:EV17.notes: Flag any plan that asks residents to conserve power during heat/cold.
ev:EV17.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV18.finding: Japan RCT: telling older adults to keep indoor temps above 24C in cold periods lowered ambulatory blood pressure ~3%.
ev:EV18.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV19.finding: Disconnections rise during extreme heat and fall on vulnerable groups; moratoria reduce disconnections; no direct causal health evaluation.
ev:EV19.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV20.finding: AC ownership correlates with lower heat mortality but programs promoting AC lack causal health evaluation; low-income US households run AC less. German hospital RCT: radiant cooling cut respiratory patients' stay by one third.
ev:EV20.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV21.finding: New Zealand RCT: non-polluting heaters raised indoor temps and cut child asthma doctor visits ~30%.
ev:EV21.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV22.finding: Greening lowers surface temperatures; causal evidence on temperature-related mortality is very limited. Tree planting/loss studies show mortality changes largely attributed to air pollution.
ev:EV22.notes: Do not credit as a heat-mortality intervention.
ev:EV22.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV25.finding: US community health center expansion: ~14% lower heat-related mortality. India community health workers: ~10% lower hot-day infant mortality. India mental health services reduced heat-related mental health harm.
ev:EV25.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV26.finding: US hospital desegregation (acute care access) nearly eliminated cold effect on Black infant mortality; community health centers showed no cold effect.
ev:EV26.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV27.finding: Mexico coverage expansion: 36% smaller moderate-cold mortality effect. Colombia: ~55% smaller cold mortality effect.
ev:EV27.notes: No US study; transport with caution.
ev:EV27.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV28.finding: Same studies: unclear effects for heat.
ev:EV28.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV29.finding: No causal evaluations; Mexico evidence shows heat-driven hospital congestion worsens outcomes, suggesting plausibility.
ev:EV29.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV35.finding: Closest reviewed evidence: targeted info campaigns; untargeted versions not evaluated.
ev:EV35.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

ev:EV36.finding: Closest reviewed evidence: Toronto cold program (null).
ev:EV36.source: Burke, Wilson et al. (2026), Understanding and addressing temperature impacts on mortality (reference numbers)

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Snow Chain Installation:
e Upon request from the department, FMSD will assist with installation of the traction enhancing device if
needed.
e lf the request is during normal Service Center operating hours, the user department is to contact their
assigned service location to schedule the installation.
e If the request is after hours, weekends or during City closures, a request via phone call to the after-
hours Fleet Emergency number QE should be made.

Vehicle Safety, Operation and Maintenance with Snow Chains:

* Tire chain/cable operating requirements vary by manufacture. Devices shall be operated and
maintained in accordance with the specific manufacture of the devices.

e Snow Chain Removal:

* Upon request from the department, once it is deemed that the traction enhancing devices are no longer
needed, the user department is to contact their assigned Service Center location to schedule the
removal.

* If the request is during normal Service Center operating hours, the user department is to contact their
assigned service location to schedule the de-installation.

If the request is after hours, weekends or during City closures, a request via phone call to the after-hours Fleet
Emergency number QE should be made.

Sheltering
The City of Austin and Travis County have situational dependent sheltering plans. Plans will be referenced
according to need.

Cold Weather Shelters (CWS)

Cold weather shelters are available for city residents once conditions are approaching a pre-determined
threshold thus resulting in the CWS activating. At that time, public facilities are identified to augment Austin
Homeless Strategies Office (HSO) operations and serve as cold weather shelters.

Emergency Public Transportation Service

Some winter storm events may require Capital Metro (CapMetro) to modify normal bus, paratransit, and rail
operations. CapMetro will modify its service based upon available resources and road/rail conditions.
Modifications may include limiting service hours, reducing service frequency, or running only certain routes. If
ice is present or anticipated, CapMetro may modify routes to avoid bridges, overpasses, and flyovers. If
conditions are severe and operator and public safety is a concern, CapMetro may suspend bus and paratransit
service entirely.

In the event of a service suspension, CapMetro will endeavour to have a limited number of buses and
paratransit vehicles available as an emergency fleet. This fleet will support life sustaining trips for Metro
Access customers and provide emergency transportation as directed by the EOC.

When weather conditions require modification of operations beyond the avoidance of overpasses, Capital
Metro will inform the AEM Duty Officer of the decision. This contact may take place in the EOC, should it be
activated, through the Capital Metro representative.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C16#1.quote: When Cold Weather Shelter activation criteria are met, HSO will coordinate with Austin Emergency Management, and community partners to support shelter operations, public messaging, and transportation assistance for individuals seeking refuge from hazardous winter weather conditions.
plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C16#1.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

During prolonged winter weather incidents, HSO will continue coordination with shelter operators, outreach
teams, and community partners to identify service gaps, monitor impacts to vulnerable populations, and
support continuity of care for individuals experiencing homelessness.

When Cold Weather Shelter activation criteria are met, HSO will coordinate with Austin Emergency
Management, and community partners to support shelter operations, public messaging, and transportation
assistance for individuals seeking refuge from hazardous winter weather conditions.

Closure Procedures

Coordination in the Closure or Modification of Government Facilities or Services

The Austin-Travis County EOC representatives will coordinate with executives for the City of Austin, Travis
County, AISD, UT, and ACC to discuss and, when possible, reach a consensus on modification of service
hours for government facilities. This information will also be available to other school districts and stakeholders
for their internal decision-making.

Key decision makers will typically coordinate actions for the upcoming business day during one or more
conferences calls through the EOC. This allows for the decision to be released to employees and the public
before they begin their trips to work or school.

Similarly, calls will be held to discuss and coordinate the need for early closures if severe weather threatens
during the day.

It must be understood that weather forecasting in Central Texas is an art and a science. At best, forecasts may
be uncertain. In some cases, it may be appropriate to delay facility opening in the morning, to allow more time
to assess actual weather conditions. This can then be followed with later announcements of closures or
“business as usual.”

An example of a typical battle rhythm schedule is included in Appendix 2.
Any conference call should include key stakeholders and a meteorologist.

¢ The Austin City Manager makes the final decision on closures for City facilities.

* The Travis County Judge makes the final decision on closures for County facilities.

* Chief Executives from other governments, schools, and organizations make the final decision on
closure of their respective facilities.

Coordination of School Closures or Modification of School Hours

The City of Austin and Travis County have worked closely with the Central Texas School Safety Consortium
(School Consortium), The University of Texas, Austin Community College, and various higher education
institutions to develop a system for coordinating the closure of schools or the modification of school hours.

The Austin Independent School District will coordinate with local School Superintendents and the School
Safety Consortium to assess their status and concerns. AISD will serve as the primary spokesperson for all K-
12 schools on the conference calls. Other school districts are welcome to monitor the calls to assist them in
their internal decision-making.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C18.quote: Consideration may be given to opening a shelter for persons dependent on electrical equipment.
plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C18.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Other Operational Considerations

Outage Management of Critical Facilities and Customers

In cases where winter storm conditions cause power failures or rotating outages the EOC will coordinate
activities to support individuals or services where the interruption of power represents a life-threatening or
safety issue.

Community members who use medical equipment that requires electrical power should have a back-up source
that can be used during a power failure. Austin Energy maintains the Medically Vulnerable Registry with
information about community members who require electricity for medical devices, etc. Consideration may be
given to opening a shelter for persons dependent on electrical equipment. The decision for opening a shelter
will be based upon recommendations from key medical stakeholders at the EOC. Priority will be based on
restoration of power, temporary solutions, and evacuation as a last resort.

City and County departments along with EOC hospital representatives and the CATRAC 7-RMOC will report
critical facilities experiencing utility outages to the Austin Energy utility representative in the EOC.

Additionally, Pedernales Electric and Bluebonnet Electric provide services to Travis County. TCOEM will
coordinate with their Emergency Response teams if needed.

Use of Chains on City of Austin Vehicles

Departments are expected to have tire traction devices to provide their respective services as needed during
an ice/snow event. The City of Austin Fleet Mobility Services (FMSD) operating procedure for snow chain
purchase, inventory, installation, and removal is as follows.

Department Responsibility:
The user department shall be responsible for budgeting and for purchase enhancing traction devices (snow
chains).
The user department shall be responsible for the storage, tracking and arrangement with FMSD for training on
installation of the traction enhancing devices (tire chains/cables).
The user department shall be responsible for providing FMSD with the following each year in October:
Identification of winter storm response units, traction devices to be used.
e Confirmation of devices on hand, any training needed.
Traction Enhancing Device (Snow Chain) will be stored on the fleet asset (unit) if possible. If not
possible the traction enhancing device (Snow Chain) will be stored in a user department-controlled
inventory location

Fleet Mobility Services Responsibility:

e FMSD shall maintain contractual, vendor and purchasing responsibilities.

e FMSD shall act as advisor and make recommendations on appropriate traction device to be purchased.
FMSD will contact departments each year during the months of October-November to confirm that
departments have established resources.

e FMSD shall provide training to user departments on the installation and de-installation of traction
enhancing devices if needed (snow chains/cables).

e FMSD will assist AFD, ATCEMS, APD as needed per user department Special Order or SOP’s outlined
for tire chains use.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C20.quote: Leads coordination of electric service restoration operations, prioritizing critical facilities, life-safety infrastructure, and community lifeline sectors (hospitals, water systems, public safety facilities, shelters, and emergency operations centers).
plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C20.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Emergency Support Function 12 — Energy
Austin Energy

Provides real-time power grid status updates, outage forecasting, and restoration prioritization
to support situational awareness and EOC decision-making.

Leads coordination of electric service restoration operations, prioritizing critical facilities, life-
safety infrastructure, and community lifeline sectors (hospitals, water systems, public safety
facilities, shelters, and emergency operations centers).

Conducts load management and grid stabilization actions during periods of extreme demand or
system stress caused by freezing temperatures.

Supports planned de-energization or isolation of electrical infrastructure when required to
protect responders, the public, and equipment during hazardous winter conditions such as
downed lines or ice damage.

Deploys crews to assess and repair damage caused by ice accumulation, wind, freezing rain, or
equipment failure.

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C23.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Public Information

Alerts and Warnings

The community will be alerted through multiple communication channels to ensure timely and accurate
information dissemination. These may include notifications from the National Weather Service (NWS) via
NOAA Weather Radio, Warn Central Texas Alerts, Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA), Integrated Public Alert
and Warning System (IPAWS), in-person notifications by first responders, and updates through media outlets
and other public information platforms. Residents are expected to take appropriate protective actions in
response to these alerts

Winter Weather Preparedness and Protective Actions
Preparedness (Year-Round)
Residents, businesses, and visitors should take proactive measures to reduce vulnerability to winter weather
hazards, including freezing temperatures, ice accumulation, power outages, and transportation disruptions.
e Register for emergency notifications through Warn Central Texas.
e Prepare an emergency supply kit ("Go-Bag") containing the 5 P's: People, Pets, Plastic (cash and credit
cards), Papers (important documents), and Prescriptions.
Maintain at least a three-day supply of food and water (one gallon per person per day).
Store flashlights, batteries, and backup charging devices.
Keep extra blankets, sleeping bags, and warm clothing readily available.
Test smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors.
Identify safe heating methods and never use grills, generators, ovens, or stovetops to heat indoor
spaces.
Maintain at least one-half tank of fuel in vehicles during winter months.
Check vehicle tires, windshield wipers, and emergency supplies.
Insulate exposed pipes and outdoor faucets.
Learn how to shut off water service at the main valve.
Identify nearby warming centers and community shelters.
Check on elderly neighbors, individuals with access and functional needs, and medically fragile
residents.
Ensure pets and livestock have adequate shelter, food, and water.
e Learn about winter weather preparedness through trusted resources such as Ready Central Texas and
the National Weather Service.

Utility Assistance and Home Weatherization Resources
Residents may reduce winter weather impacts through utility assistance and energy-efficiency programs
designed to improve household resilience.
e The City of Austin Customer Assistance Program (CAP) provides utility bill discounts and assistance for
eligible low- and fixed-income households.
e The Texas Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) helps eligible households improve home energy
efficiency through insulation, weather sealing, and other weatherization measures that reduce energy
costs and improve indoor comfort during extreme temperatures.

Additional information is available through:
e City of Austin Utility Bill Discounts Program
e Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs Weatherization Assistance Program

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C24.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Concept of Operations

The following strategy has been developed by the participating agencies that are involved in winter weather
response:

e Each participating agency will monitor potential weather conditions and will notify other agencies when
conditions are warranted.

e Coordination among agencies will be handled at the City of Austin-Travis County Emergency
Operations Center (EOC). Each agency shown on the notification sequence will send a representative
to the EOC when it is activated. Prior to the EOC being activated, the City of Austin and Travis County
may coordinate pre-incident situational awareness messages and meetings. Virtual options for
coordination may be taken into consideration depending on the response.

e Once activated, each agency will advise the EOC, through their representative, of all winter related
impacts like road closures, power outages, reduction in services, and other major incidents. Agencies
will notify the EOC when winter related impacts have ended, or services restored like roads are
reopened.

e The EOC will disseminate information regarding road closures as appropriate.

Every attempt will be made to coordinate any modification of hours between major government entities
and school districts. Modification of hours includes early closing, late opening, or closure for the day.
The primary method for coordination of closure will be through a conference call established through
the Austin-Travis County EOC. The conference call will include decision makers from the City of Austin,
Travis County, University of Texas (UT), Austin Independent School District (AISD), Austin Community
College (ACC), and other school districts or governmental entities as deemed appropriate. School
closures place a burden on healthcare facilities and critical infrastructure employees who have children
but need to report to work.

e The use of the Austin Warning and Communications System (AWACS) city/county all-call page will be
considered for the dissemination of government closures or delayed openings. This would include, but
not necessarily be limited to, the City of Austin, Travis County, AISD, ACC, and the University of Texas.
Consideration will be given to the use of AWACS for reporting changes to events with more than
25,000 individuals (including event staff).

e The EOC will not attempt to disseminate individual schools (private and smaller public districts) and
event closures (less than 25,000 in attendance) to the media. That should be done directly by the
district involved.

e The EOC will work with departments to pre-position resources such as mission ready sheltering
packages before the incident.

EOC Activation

During the pre-event and initial stages of any potential winter weather event, the Austin AEM Duty Officer will
serve as the focal point for the communication of weather and operational information as it relates to winter
weather operations. Winter weather incidents will generally be managed through the Austin/Travis County
Emergency Operations Center utilizing Emergency Support Function (ESF) coordination. Field operations will
remain under the authority of the responsible agencies and departments. Incident Command may be
established for specific tactical incidents requiring on-scene management. Area Command may be considered
during exceptionally complex winter weather events involving multiple Incident Command organizations
operating simultaneously across multiple jurisdictions or operational areas.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C31.quote: Adjust thermostats to maintain safe indoor temperatures.
plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C31.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

Actions Before a Winter Weather Event
When winter weather is forecast:

e Monitor National Weather Service forecasts and local emergency information.
Stay informed on winter weather danger levels and expected conditions.
Ensure family members and employees understand emergency and evacuation plans.
Cover or drain irrigation systems.
Open cabinet doors beneath sinks to allow warm air circulation around pipes.
Drip indoor faucets to reduce the risk of frozen pipes.
Bring pets indoors.
Charge electronic devices, medical equipment, and backup batteries.
Complete errands and obtain necessary supplies before precipitation begins.
Avoid unnecessary travel.
Identify alternate travel routes in case bridges or overpasses become impassable.
Locate flashlights and emergency supplies.
Adjust thermostats to maintain safe indoor temperatures.

Protective Actions During Winter Weather
During freezing conditions, ice events, or prolonged power outages:

e Follow instructions from emergency responders and local officials.
Avoid travel unless absolutely necessary.
Treat signalized intersections without power as four-way stops.
Avoid walking on ice-covered surfaces.
Use generators outdoors only and at least 20 feet from buildings.
Keep space heaters away from combustible materials.
Close off unused rooms to conserve heat.
Wear layered clothing and use blankets to maintain body temperature.
Move vulnerable household members to the warmest interior room.
Monitor indoor temperatures; temperatures below 55°F increase the likelihood of frozen pipes.
Continue checking on neighbors and vulnerable populations.

Water System and Utility Disruption Safety
If freezing temperatures damage water infrastructure:
e Shut off the water supply if a pipe bursts.
e Use stored water for drinking and sanitation needs.
e Follow all boil water notices and public health guidance issued by local authorities.

Winter Driving Safety
If travel cannot be avoided:
e Drive slowly and increase following distance.
e Avoid sudden braking, acceleration, or sharp turns.
e Watch for black ice, particularly on bridges, overpasses, and shaded roadways.
e Carry emergency supplies in vehicles, including blankets, water, food, flashlights, and phone chargers.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C32.quote: the City of Austin Homeless Strategy Office (HSO) will coordinate with Austin Emergency Management (AEM), nonprofit service providers, faith-based organizations, and regional partners to conduct proactive outreach and connect individuals to available services and shelter resources.
plan:4805000_EOPX_2026_C32.page_text:
Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-8471-83CE-9590E85FD087

WINTER WEATHER

Hazard-Specific Annex

e Coordinating resource requests and mutual aid support through local, regional, and state resource
management systems.
Sharing information on utility outages, restoration priorities, and impacts to critical infrastructure.

e Coordinating public information messaging to provide consistent and timely information to residents
throughout the region.

e Identifying regional impacts to healthcare facilities, long-term care facilities, schools, and other critical
services.

e Coordinating transportation and access issues affecting commuters and travelers moving between
Travis, Hays, and Williamson Counties.

e Supporting regional planning for commodity distribution, emergency protective measures, and recovery
operations during prolonged outages or infrastructure disruptions.

During widespread winter weather events, Austin/Travis County may participate in regional coordination calls
with Hays County, Williamson County, TDEM, utility providers, transportation agencies, and other stakeholders
to establish a common operating picture and identify resource shortfalls requiring state assistance. When local
and regional resources become strained, requests for assistance may be submitted through TDEM in
accordance with established emergency management procedures.

Outreach to Vulnerable Populations

Individuals experiencing homelessness are among the populations most vulnerable to winter weather hazards
due to prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures, limited access to shelter, and increased risk of cold-

Emergency number QE should be made.

Sheltering
The City of Austin and Travis County have situational dependent sheltering plans. Plans will be referenced
according to need.

Cold Weather Shelters (CWS)

Cold weather shelters are available for city residents once conditions are approaching a pre-determined
threshold thus resulting in the CWS activating. At that time, public facilities are identified to augment Austin
Homeless Strategies Office (HSO) operations and serve as cold weather shelters.

Emergency Public Transportation Service

Some winter storm events may require Capital Metro (CapMetro) to modify normal bus, paratransit, and rail
operations. CapMetro will modify its service based upon available resources and road/rail conditions.
Modifications may include limiting service hours, reducing service frequency, or running only certain routes. If
ice is present or anticipated, CapMetro may modify routes to avoid bridges, overpasses, and flyovers. If
conditions are severe and operator and public safety is a concern, CapMetro may suspend bus and paratransit
service entirely.

In the event of a service suspension, CapMetro will endeavour to have a limited number of buses and
paratransit vehicles available as an emergency fleet. This fleet will support life sustaining trips for Metro
Access customers and provide emergency transportation as directed by the EOC.

When weather conditions require modification of operations beyond the avoidance of overpasses, Capital
Metro will inform the AEM Duty Officer of the decision. This contact may take place in the EOC, should it be
activated, through the Capital Metro representative.

During prolonged winter weather incidents, HSO will continue coordination with shelter operators, outreach
teams, and community partners to identify service gaps, monitor impacts to vulnerable populations, and
support continuity of care for individuals experiencing homelessness.

When Cold Weather Shelter activation criteria are met, HSO will coordinate with Austin Emergency
Management, and community partners to support shelter operations, public messaging, and transportation
assistance for individuals seeking refuge from hazardous winter weather conditions.

Closure Procedures

Coordination in the Closure or Modification of Government Facilities or Services

The Austin-Travis County EOC representatives will coordinate with executives for the City of Austin, Travis
County, AISD, UT, and ACC to discuss and, when possible, reach a consensus on modification of service
hours for government facilities. This information will also be available to other school districts and stakeholders
for their internal decision-making.

Key decision makers will typically coordinate actions for the upcoming business day during one or more
conferences calls through the EOC. This allows for the decision to be released to employees and the public
before they begin their trips to work or school.

Similarly, calls will be held to discuss and coordinate the need for early closures if severe weather threatens
during the day.

It must be understood that weather forecasting in Central Texas is an art and a science. At best, forecasts may
be uncertain. In some cases, it may be appropriate to delay facility opening in the morning, to allow more time
to assess actual weather conditions. This can then be followed with later announcements of closures or
“business as usual.”

An example of a typical battle rhythm schedule is included in Appendix 2.
Any conference call should include key stakeholders and a meteorologist.

¢ The Austin City Manager makes the final decision on closures for City facilities.

* The Travis County Judge makes the final decision on closures for County facilities.

* Chief Executives from other governments, schools, and organizations make the final decision on
closure of their respective facilities.

Coordination of School Closures or Modification of School Hours

The City of Austin and Travis County have worked closely with the Central Texas School Safety Consortium
(School Consortium), The University of Texas, Austin Community College, and various higher education
institutions to develop a system for coordinating the closure of schools or the modification of school hours.

The Austin Independent School District will coordinate with local School Superintendents and the School
Safety Consortium to assess their status and concerns. AISD will serve as the primary spokesperson for all K-
12 schools on the conference calls. Other school districts are welcome to monitor the calls to assist them in
their internal decision-making.

Critical Facilities and Vulnerable Populations

Winter weather hazards disproportionately impact vulnerable populations, including individuals experiencing
homelessness, older adults, medically fragile individuals, and those without reliable heating. Access to
warming centers, medical care, and essential services may be constrained by hazardous travel conditions.
Power outages and water service disruptions further increase risk to life safety and necessitate coordinated
sheltering, transportation, and outreach operations.

Interagency Coordination and Operational Impacts

Winter weather events place simultaneous demands on transportation, utilities, public safety, health services,
and emergency management functions. Reduced staffing availability, hazardous travel conditions, and
competing response priorities can strain resources across departments. Pre-identified vulnerabilities, access
constraints, and infrastructure risks must be incorporated into planning assumptions to support timely decision-
making, resource allocation, and public messaging during winter weather incidents.

Community Assistance and Human Services Considerations

Residents affected by disasters may experience financial hardship due to increased utility usage, damaged
housing, or loss of income. The City of Austin and the State of Texas offer programs that can help eligible
households reduce utility costs and improve home energy efficiency.

e The City of Austin Utilities Customer Assistance Program (CAP) provides utility bill discounts for
qualifying low- and fixed-income households, reducing annual utility costs through discounts on electric,
water, wastewater, and drainage services. Emergency utility payment assistance may also be available
through the Plus 1 Program. Link

e The Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) Weatherization Assistance
Program (WAP) helps eligible low-income households’ lower energy costs through energy-efficiency
improvements such as insulation, weather sealing, and other home weatherizalion measures. The
program is intended to reduce long-term energy burdens and increase housing resilience. Link

Assumptions

Emergency Operations Center (EOC) Activation

During a significant winter weather event—including freezing rain, sleet, snow, or prolonged hard freeze
conditions—the City of Austin and Travis County may experience widespread transportation disruptions, utility
failures, and increased life-safety risks. In such an event, the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) may be
activated to coordinate interdepartmental operations, support resource allocation, and manage public
information.

EOC activation may be triggered by issuance of National Weather Service Winter Storm Watches or Warnings,
forecasted ice accumulation, extended subfreezing temperatures, or observed impacts exceeding routine
departmental capacity. A local disaster declaration may be issued to facilitate emergency protective measures,
emergency procurement, shelter operations, and access to state or federal assistance.

Command and Coordination

Incident Command Structure (ICS)

The Austin Emergency Management Director, or designee, will manage the Emergency Operations Center
(EOC) and provide coordinated support to Incident Command throughout the incident. AEM declares the EOC
activation level based on conditions and forecasts, coordinates EOC briefings, and communicates goals and
objectives that support on-scene command for each operational period.

Using available threat and hazard information, Incident Command will initiate protective action measures.
Evacuation decisions and should follow procedures outlined in the Functional Annex: All-Hazards Protective
Action Plan.

Incident Priorities

1. Life Safety: Protecting the public, responders, and vulnerable populations (e.g., unhoused individuals,
medically dependent persons, elderly residents) is the highest priority. Actions include sheltering,
warming operations, medical support, traffic incident response, and public warning.

2. Incident Stabilization: Stabilizing winter weather impacts by maintaining situational awareness,
coordinating multi-agency response, restoring critical lifelines (power, transportation, communications,
water), and preventing secondary incidents such as crashes, fires, or carbon monoxide exposure.

3. Property and Environmental Conservation: Protecting homes, businesses, and critical infrastructure
systems from damage caused by freezing temperatures, ice accumulation, snow load, and utility
disruptions. Emphasis includes infrastructure protection, burst pipe prevention, and continuity of
essential services.

4. Societal Restoration: Supporting rapid recovery and return to normal operations through debris/ice
removal, utility restoration, reopening transportation networks, and resumption of government,
healthcare, education, and commerce functions.

Roles and Responsibilities Per Emergency Support Functions

Emergency Support Function 1 — Transportation
Austin Transportation and Public Works

e Supports coordination of traffic management operations during winter weather conditions,
including roadway monitoring, closure implementation, and detour routing.

e Deploys and maintain traffic control devices, minimal barricades, signage, and signal systems to
support safe travel and incident scene protection during icy or hazardous road conditions to
assist APD.

e Prioritize treatment and access for critical transportation corridors, including emergency routes,
hospital access routes bridges, and elevated roadways.

e Supports post-incident damage assessments and safety inspections of transportation
infrastructure affected by freezing temperatures, ice accumulation, or storm impacts.

e Provides trained personnel to assist with field assessments, route clearance coordination, and
operational support as requested.

Austin Fleet Mobility Services

e Provides transportation fleet support for City personnel conducting winter weather response and

recovery operations.

Activation Triggers

Activation of the EOC for winter weather events will be coordinated through the AEM Director and TCOEM
Emergency Management Coordinator. Austin AEM and Travis County Office of Emergency Management
(TCOEM) will assess and monitor the situation. When practical, participating in City, County, and State
agencies will be consulted prior to issuing an activation notice. For the safety of EOC responders, when
possible, the EOC will be activated prior to the onset of winter precipitation in Travis County. Any activation
could include the agencies and entities found in Appendix 3 — Winter Weather EOC Agencies.

Role of the EOC

The Austin-Travis County EOC will serve as the location for coordination of all Austin and Travis County
government activities related to winter storm operations. This includes, but is not limited to, the following:

* Ensure operation of critical governmental operations, including public safety and utility crews.

* Facilitate situational awareness conference calls.

* Coordinate road surface treatment operations within Travis County.

* Coordinate the decision making on the closing and opening of publicly maintained roads.

* Collect and assess information including weather reports, observed conditions, and damage reports.

* Assess the impact of storms on community safety and governmental operations.

* Coordination for the decision to modify the hours of operation for the City of Austin, Travis County,

University of Texas, AISD, ACC, and other key stakeholders.

* Coordination of mass care and sheltering and warming centers.

* Coordinate impact to Cold Weather Shelter (CWS) operations if activated.

* Coordinate the release of public information.

* Coordinate recovery planning upon EOC activation.

Regional Coordination

Winter weather incidents frequently produce impacts that extend beyond jurisdictional boundaries and affect
communities throughout Central Texas simultaneously. Because severe winter weather can impact
transportation networks, utility systems, critical infrastructure, and vulnerable populations across multiple
counties, coordinated regional response efforts are essential.

The City of Austin and Travis County will maintain close coordination with neighboring jurisdictions, including
Hays County and Williamson County, to support a unified regional response and recovery effort. Coordination
may occur through established emergency management channels, regional coordination calls, Emergency
Operations Centers (EOCs), the Capital Area Council of Governments (CAPCOG), the Texas Division of
Emergency Management (TDEM), and other partner agencies as appropriate.

Regional coordination activities may include:
e Sharing situational awareness information, weather forecasts, damage assessments, and operational
priorities.
e¢ Coordinating roadway treatment operations, closures, detours, and public messaging across
jurisdictional boundaries.

e Exchanging information regarding shelter and warming center availability, capacity, and access
requirements.

Snow Chain Installation:
e Upon request from the department, FMSD will assist with installation of the traction enhancing device if
needed.
e lf the request is during normal Service Center operating hours, the user department is to contact their
assigned service location to schedule the installation.
e If the request is after hours, weekends or during City closures, a request via phone call to the after-
hours Fleet Emergency number QE should be made.

Vehicle Safety, Operation and Maintenance with Snow Chains:

* Tire chain/cable operating requirements vary by manufacture. Devices shall be operated and
maintained in accordance with the specific manufacture of the devices.

e Snow Chain Removal:

* Upon request from the department, once it is deemed that the traction enhancing devices are no longer
needed, the user department is to contact their assigned Service Center location to schedule the
removal.

* If the request is during normal Service Center operating hours, the user department is to contact their
assigned service location to schedule the de-installation.

If the request is after hours, weekends or during City closures, a request via phone call to the after-hours Fleet
Emergency number QE should be made.

Sheltering
The City of Austin and Travis County have situational dependent sheltering plans. Plans will be referenced
according to need.

Cold Weather Shelters (CWS)

Cold weather shelters are available for city residents once conditions are approaching a pre-determined
threshold thus resulting in the CWS activating. At that time, public facilities are identified to augment Austin
Homeless Strategies Office (HSO) operations and serve as cold weather shelters.

Emergency Public Transportation Service

Some winter storm events may require Capital Metro (CapMetro) to modify normal bus, paratransit, and rail
operations. CapMetro will modify its service based upon available resources and road/rail conditions.
Modifications may include limiting service hours, reducing service frequency, or running only certain routes. If
ice is present or anticipated, CapMetro may modify routes to avoid bridges, overpasses, and flyovers. If
conditions are severe and operator and public safety is a concern, CapMetro may suspend bus and paratransit
service entirely.

In the event of a service suspension, CapMetro will endeavour to have a limited number of buses and
paratransit vehicles available as an emergency fleet. This fleet will support life sustaining trips for Metro
Access customers and provide emergency transportation as directed by the EOC.

When weather conditions require modification of operations beyond the avoidance of overpasses, Capital
Metro will inform the AEM Duty Officer of the decision. This contact may take place in the EOC, should it be
activated, through the Capital Metro representative.

During widespread winter weather events, Austin/Travis County may participate in regional coordination calls

Outreach to Vulnerable Populations

Individuals experiencing homelessness are among the populations most vulnerable to winter weather hazards
due to prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures, limited access to shelter, and increased risk of cold-
related illness or death. As winter weather conditions are forecast, the City of Austin Homeless Strategy Office
(HSO) will coordinate with Austin Emergency Management (AEM), nonprofit service providers, faith-based
organizations, and regional partners to conduct proactive outreach and connect individuals to available
services and shelter resources.

Prior to anticipated freezing temperatures, HSO may:

Coordinate enhanced outreach operations to areas known to have unsheltered populations.
Disseminate information regarding anticipated weather conditions, warming center locations, shelter
availability, transportation options, and cold weather safety measures.

e Coordinate with service providers to encourage voluntary relocation to shelters, warming centers, or
other safe indoor facilities.

e Support transportation efforts for individuals seeking access to warming centers or emergency shelter.
Coordinate the distribution of cold-weather supplies such as blankets, cold-weather clothing, hand
warmers, and other protective items as available.

e Maintain situational awareness regarding shelter capacity and communicate resource needs to the
Emergency Operations Center (EOC) when activated.

e Coordinate with healthcare, behavioral health, and social service partners to identify individuals with
elevated medical or functional needs who may require additional assistance during extreme cold
events.

Docusign Envelope ID: 88D11EA2-7760-847 1-83CE-9590E85FD087

Hazard-Specific Annex

when hazardous winter weather is imminent or occurring and poses a serious threat to life and property. These
products serve as primary decision-support tools for emergency management agencies and partner
organizations.

Winter storms vary significantly in duration, intensity, and geographic extent. Some events may consist of light
wintry precipitation over a few hours, while others may persist for several days and affect large portions of the
state. Winter storms are often accompanied by strong winds and reduced visibility, further exacerbating
transportation hazards and complicating emergency response and recovery operations.

In the Austin area, significant wintry precipitation, defined as freezing rain, sleet, or snow sufficient to cause
substantial impacts to travel and daily activities, occurs on average approximately once every two years. The
largest recorded snowstorm occurred on November 22—23, 1937, when approximately 11 inches of snow were
recorded. More recently, the February 14-15, 2021 winter storm produced 6.4 inches of snow at Austin
Bergstrom International Airport and Austin Mabry, accompanied by prolonged freezing temperatures that
resulted in widespread power outages, water system failures, and cascading impacts across multiple sectors.

Normal winter precipitation (December—February) in Austin averages approximately 7.25 inches, accounting
for roughly 20 percent of annual precipitation. Winter weather in Central Texas is highly variable, and periods
of extreme cold may be interspersed with unusually warm winter days. This variability complicates forecasting,
preparedness activities, and public messaging efforts.

(Source)

Winter weather hazards pose a significant risk to life safety, critical infrastructure, and continuity of operations.
Ice accumulation and freezing temperatures can overwhelm transportation networks, disrupt utility services,
strain emergency response capabilities, and disproportionately impact vulnerable populations. Coordinated
preparedness, timely warnings, and effective response planning are essential to reduce the cascading effects
of winter weather events across the community.

Hazard Definition

A freeze is defined as meteorological conditions in which temperatures fall to or below 32°F (0°C), allowing ice
formation on surfaces and infrastructure. Such conditions in Central Texas are typically associated with strong
Arctic fronts and rapid temperature drops.

Regional Climate Characteristics
Austin has a humid subtropical climate with generally mild winters, though periodic cold outbreaks occur.
e Winters are typically mild, but below-freezing temperatures occur about 25 days per year on average.
(Source)
e AtCamp Mabry, sub-freezing temperatures occur about 12 days annually, while Austin-Bergstrom
Airport averages about 33 days. (Source)
e Strong northerly winds associated with winter cold fronts can cause rapid temperature drops and
sudden freezes. (Source)
e Typical winter minimum temperatures in Austin during January—February average in the mid-30s °F,
with occasional records significantly lower. (Source)

These characteristics indicate winter weather is infrequent but operationally significant when it occurs.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026

Other Operational Considerations

Outage Management of Critical Facilities and Customers

In cases where winter storm conditions cause power failures or rotating outages the EOC will coordinate
activities to support individuals or services where the interruption of power represents a life-threatening or
safety issue.

Community members who use medical equipment that requires electrical power should have a back-up source
that can be used during a power failure. Austin Energy maintains the Medically Vulnerable Registry with
information about community members who require electricity for medical devices, etc. Consideration may be
given to opening a shelter for persons dependent on electrical equipment. The decision for opening a shelter
will be based upon recommendations from key medical stakeholders at the EOC. Priority will be based on
restoration of power, temporary solutions, and evacuation as a last resort.

City and County departments along with EOC hospital representatives and the CATRAC 7-RMOC will report
critical facilities experiencing utility outages to the Austin Energy utility representative in the EOC.

Additionally, Pedernales Electric and Bluebonnet Electric provide services to Travis County. TCOEM will
coordinate with their Emergency Response teams if needed.

Use of Chains on City of Austin Vehicles

Departments are expected to have tire traction devices to provide their respective services as needed during
an ice/snow event. The City of Austin Fleet Mobility Services (FMSD) operating procedure for snow chain
purchase, inventory, installation, and removal is as follows.

Department Responsibility:
The user department shall be responsible for budgeting and for purchase enhancing traction devices (snow
chains).
The user department shall be responsible for the storage, tracking and arrangement with FMSD for training on
installation of the traction enhancing devices (tire chains/cables).
The user department shall be responsible for providing FMSD with the following each year in October:
Identification of winter storm response units, traction devices to be used.
e Confirmation of devices on hand, any training needed.
Traction Enhancing Device (Snow Chain) will be stored on the fleet asset (unit) if possible. If not
possible the traction enhancing device (Snow Chain) will be stored in a user department-controlled
inventory location

Fleet Mobility Services Responsibility:

e FMSD shall maintain contractual, vendor and purchasing responsibilities.

e FMSD shall act as advisor and make recommendations on appropriate traction device to be purchased.
FMSD will contact departments each year during the months of October-November to confirm that
departments have established resources.

e FMSD shall provide training to user departments on the installation and de-installation of traction
enhancing devices if needed (snow chains/cables).

e FMSD will assist AFD, ATCEMS, APD as needed per user department Special Order or SOP’s outlined
for tire chains use.

JN Austin Updated: April 30, 2026
